body:
How Light Makes Vision Possible

Light is a form of electromagnetic radiation. The portion detectable by the human eye is called visible light. We see an object when light coming from that object enters our eyes.

A luminous object produces its own light. Examples include the Sun, a glowing electric lamp and a burning candle. A non-luminous object, such as a book, chair or the Moon, becomes visible mainly because it reflects light from another source.

In a uniform transparent medium, light travels along straight lines. This property is called rectilinear propagation of light. It explains the formation of shadows and provides the foundation for drawing ray diagrams.

Rays and Beams of Light

A ray of light is an imaginary straight line showing the direction in which light travels. A collection of rays forms a beam. Rays are used to represent the paths of light in reflection, refraction and image formation.

When light encounters a surface, some of it may be reflected, some may pass through the material, and some may be absorbed. The proportions depend on the material and the conditions.

Reflection of Light

Reflection is the change in direction of light when it returns into the medium from which it approached a surface.

A polished mirror reflects light in an orderly manner. A sheet of ordinary paper also reflects light, but its uneven surface sends the reflected rays in different directions.

The 2 Laws of Reflection

Consider a ray of light striking a plane mirror. The ray approaching the surface is the incident ray, and the ray leaving after reflection is the reflected ray. The perpendicular drawn to the surface at the point of incidence is called the normal.

  1. First law: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
  2. Second law: The incident ray, reflected ray and normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane.

Both angles are measured from the normal, not from the reflecting surface. If the incident ray makes an angle of 35° with the normal, the reflected ray also makes an angle of 35° with the normal.

Mathematically, the first law is written as:

$$i=r$$

When light falls along the normal, its angle of incidence is 0°. It is reflected back along the same path.

Regular and Diffused Reflection

Regular Reflection

When parallel incident rays fall on a smooth plane reflecting surface, the reflected rays remain parallel. This is called regular or specular reflection. A sufficiently smooth mirror produces a clear image because light from different points of an object is reflected in an orderly manner.

Diffused Reflection

When parallel rays fall on an irregular surface, they are reflected in different directions because the local normal changes from point to point. This is called diffused or irregular reflection. It allows us to see ordinary objects from different viewing directions.

Diffused reflection does not violate the laws of reflection. At every point on the rough surface, the angle of incidence still equals the angle of reflection when measured from the local normal.

The laws of reflection apply to plane, concave and convex reflecting surfaces. Curvature changes the direction of the local normal and therefore the final direction of the reflected rays.

Prelims focus

  • Light travels in straight lines in a uniform transparent medium.
  • The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
  • Both angles are measured from the normal.
  • The incident ray, reflected ray and normal are coplanar.
  • Regular reflection occurs on smooth surfaces; diffused reflection occurs on irregular surfaces.
  • Trap: Diffused reflection does not mean that the laws of reflection fail.

[NCERT, Science, Class VI, Chapter 11, 'Light, Shadows and Reflections', printed pp. 107–113; NCERT, Science, Class VIII, Chapter 16, 'Light', Sections 16.1–16.3, printed pp. 199–203.]

title: Light, Its Propagation and the Laws of Reflection

body:
What Is a Plane Mirror?

A plane mirror has a flat reflecting surface. It produces an image when light from an object reflects from the mirror and reaches the observer's eyes.

The reflected rays obey the laws of reflection. To the observer, the rays appear to originate from a position behind the mirror. This apparent position determines where the image is seen.

Real and Virtual Images

A real image is formed where light rays actually meet after reflection or refraction. It can be obtained on a screen placed at that position.

A virtual image is formed where light rays appear to meet when their paths are extended backward. The rays do not actually meet there, so the image cannot be obtained on a screen.

A plane mirror always produces a virtual image of a real object placed in front of it. The reflected rays spread out toward the observer, but their backward extensions meet at the apparent image position behind the mirror.

Characteristics of the Image Formed by a Plane Mirror

  • Virtual: The reflected rays do not actually meet at the image position.
  • Erect: The image is upright rather than upside down.
  • Same size: Image height equals object height.
  • Equal distance: The image lies as far behind the mirror as the object lies in front of it.
  • Laterally inverted: The object's apparent left and right sides are interchanged when viewed in the mirror.

The magnification of a plane mirror is +1. Magnification compares image height with object height. The positive sign indicates an erect image, while the magnitude 1 indicates equal size.

Object Distance and Image Distance

Suppose an object is placed 2 m in front of a plane mirror. Its image appears 2 m behind the mirror. Therefore, the distance between the object and its image is 4 m.

For a stationary plane mirror, if the object moves 1 m closer to the mirror, the image also moves 1 m closer to the mirror on the opposite side. Their separation decreases by 2 m.

Lateral Inversion

In a plane mirror, the right side of an object appears on the left side of its image, and the left side appears on the right. This effect is called lateral inversion.

For example, when a person raises the right hand, the reflected person appears to raise the left hand. However, the head remains above the feet. Lateral inversion is not the same as vertical inversion.

The word AMBULANCE is commonly written in reversed form on the front of an ambulance so that drivers ahead can read it correctly in their rear-view mirrors.

Multiple Reflection by Plane Mirrors

A reflected ray can strike another mirror and undergo reflection again. This principle is called multiple reflection.

In a simple periscope, 2 appropriately positioned plane mirrors reflect light successively, allowing an observer to see an object that is not in the direct line of sight.

Two inclined plane mirrors can form multiple images. For an object placed symmetrically between 2 plane mirrors inclined at 90°, 3 images are obtained under the usual ideal arrangement. The number of images depends on the angle between the mirrors and, in some arrangements, the object's position.

A plane mirror does not turn a real object upside down or make its image smaller. Its image is always virtual, erect, equal in size and laterally inverted.

Prelims focus

  • A plane mirror produces a virtual, erect image.
  • Object distance equals image distance from the mirror.
  • Magnification of a plane mirror is +1.
  • At an object distance of 2 m, object-image separation is 4 m.
  • Lateral inversion means apparent left-right interchange.
  • Trap: A virtual image cannot be projected onto a screen placed at its apparent position.

[NCERT, Science, Class VII, Chapter 15, 'Light', Section 15.2, printed pp. 175–179; NCERT, Science, Class VIII, Chapter 16, 'Light', Sections 16.2–16.5, printed pp. 201–204; NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Section 9.1, printed p. 135.]

pictures.caption: A plane mirror forms a virtual image at the same perpendicular distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.

title: Plane Mirrors: Image Formation, Lateral Inversion and Applications

body:
Meaning of a Spherical Mirror

A spherical mirror is a mirror whose reflecting surface forms part of a spherical surface. According to the direction of curvature of the reflecting surface, spherical mirrors are divided into concave and convex mirrors.

Concave Mirror

A concave mirror has a reflecting surface curved inward, toward the centre of the sphere of which it forms a part. It is also called a converging mirror because rays arriving parallel to its principal axis are reflected toward a common point.

The hollow inner surface of a polished spoon approximately behaves like a concave mirror.

Convex Mirror

A convex mirror has a reflecting surface curved outward. It is also called a diverging mirror because incident rays parallel to its principal axis are reflected in different directions and appear to originate from a point behind the mirror.

The outwardly bulging surface of a polished spoon approximately behaves like a convex mirror.

Important Terms Used for Spherical Mirrors

  • Pole (P): The geometrical centre of the reflecting surface of the mirror.
  • Centre of curvature (C): The centre of the sphere of which the reflecting surface is a part. It lies in front of a concave mirror and behind a convex mirror.
  • Radius of curvature (R): The radius of that sphere, equal in magnitude to the distance between P and C.
  • Principal axis: The straight line passing through P and C. It is normal to the mirror at its pole.
  • Principal focus (F): The point on the principal axis where rays initially parallel to the principal axis meet after reflection from a concave mirror, or from which they appear to diverge after reflection from a convex mirror.
  • Focal length (f): The distance between the pole and the principal focus.
  • Aperture: The effective diameter of the reflecting surface.

Relationship Between Focal Length and Radius of Curvature

For a spherical mirror having a small aperture compared with its radius of curvature, the principal focus lies approximately halfway between the pole and centre of curvature.

$$R=2f$$

When distances are treated as positive magnitudes, this means that focal length is half the radius of curvature. The relationship also holds with the corresponding signed distances under the New Cartesian Sign Convention.

For example, a spherical mirror with a radius of curvature of magnitude 30 cm has a focal length of magnitude 15 cm.

Principal Rays Used in Mirror Diagrams

Images formed by spherical mirrors can be located by tracing 2 appropriately chosen rays from the same point of an object.

  1. Ray parallel to the principal axis: After reflection, it passes through F for a concave mirror. For a convex mirror, its backward extension passes through F behind the mirror.
  2. Ray through or directed toward F: After reflection, it travels parallel to the principal axis.
  3. Ray through or directed toward C: It strikes the mirror along the local normal and is reflected back along its original path.
  4. Ray incident at P: It is reflected according to the laws of reflection, making equal angles with the principal axis at the pole.

These ray rules are applications of the laws of reflection. The directions of reflected rays are determined by the local normal at the point where each ray strikes the mirror.

The centre of curvature is not a point on the reflecting surface. For a concave mirror, C and F lie in front of the mirror. For a convex mirror, C and F lie behind the mirror.

Prelims focus

  • Concave mirrors converge rays parallel to the principal axis.
  • Convex mirrors diverge rays parallel to the principal axis.
  • P denotes pole, C denotes centre of curvature and F denotes principal focus.
  • For a spherical mirror of small aperture, R = 2f.
  • A ray directed along the normal returns along the same path.
  • Trap: A convex mirror's focus is virtual, although it is represented by the same symbol F.

[NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Sections 9.2–9.2.2, printed pp. 135–139, especially Figures 9.1–9.6.]

pictures.alt: Concave rays meet at a real focus in front; convex rays diverge from a virtual focus behind. Both show P, F, C and R = 2f.
pictures.caption: The principal focus is in front of a concave mirror and behind a convex mirror.

title: Spherical Mirrors: Concave and Convex Surfaces, Focus and Ray Rules

body:
Why Object Position Matters

A concave mirror reflects light toward its principal axis, but the nature and size of the image depend on the object's position relative to the pole P, principal focus F and centre of curvature C.

For an object sufficiently far from the mirror, reflected rays can meet in front of the mirror to form a real and inverted image. When the object is placed between the pole and principal focus, the reflected rays diverge and their backward extensions meet behind the mirror. The resulting image is virtual, erect and enlarged.

6 Standard Positions of the Object

Object positionImage positionRelative sizeNature
At infinityAt FHighly diminishedReal, inverted
Beyond CBetween C and FDiminishedReal, inverted
At CAt CSame sizeReal, inverted
Between C and FBeyond CEnlargedReal, inverted
At FAt infinityHighly enlargedReal, inverted in the ideal ray model
Between F and PBehind the mirrorEnlargedVirtual, erect

Real Images Formed by a Concave Mirror

Object Beyond the Centre of Curvature

When an object is beyond C, a ray parallel to the principal axis reflects through F. Another ray directed through C returns along its original path. Their reflected paths meet between C and F.

Therefore, the image is real, inverted and smaller than the object. It can be obtained on a screen placed at the image position.

Object at the Centre of Curvature

When the object is placed at C, the image is also formed at C. It is real, inverted and equal in size to the object.

Object Between C and F

When the object moves between C and F, the reflected rays meet beyond C. The image becomes real, inverted and larger than the object.

Object at the Principal Focus

When the object is at F, rays leaving the mirror from a given object point emerge parallel in the ideal ray model. Their image is therefore described as forming at infinity and being highly enlarged.

In this position, a sharp image cannot be obtained on a screen placed at a finite distance from the mirror.

Virtual Image Formed by a Concave Mirror

When the object is placed between F and P, the reflected rays diverge. Their backward extensions meet behind the mirror, producing a virtual, erect and enlarged image.

This is the principle behind using a concave mirror as a shaving or makeup mirror. The face must be sufficiently close to the mirror, within its focal length, to obtain an upright enlarged image.

Applications of Concave Mirrors

  • Shaving and makeup mirrors: Produce enlarged, erect images when the face is within the focal length.
  • Dentists' mirrors: Can produce enlarged, upright images of nearby teeth.
  • Torches, searchlights and vehicle headlights: A light source placed near the focus produces an approximately parallel reflected beam.
  • Solar furnaces: Large concave mirrors concentrate approximately parallel sunlight into a small region, producing high temperatures.

A concave mirror does not always produce a real image. For a real object placed between P and F, the image is virtual, erect and enlarged.

Prelims focus

  • Beyond C: real, inverted and diminished image between C and F.
  • At C: real, inverted image of equal size at C.
  • Between C and F: real, inverted and enlarged image beyond C.
  • At F: image at infinity in the ideal ray model.
  • Between P and F: virtual, erect and enlarged image behind the mirror.
  • Trap: A concave mirror is converging, but the image formed for an object within F is virtual.

[NCERT, Science, Class X, Chapter 9, Sections 9.2.1–9.2.2, Table 9.1 and Figure 9.7, printed pp. 137–140.]
